title: How is SMA inherited? A clear guide for families
excerpt: Understand SMN1-related SMA inheritance, carrier parents, the chance in each pregnancy, family testing and why a negative carrier screen needs context.
intro: In the usual inheritance pattern for SMN1-related SMA, both parents are carriers. Each pregnancy then has a one-in-four chance of a child with SMA. That chance applies afresh each time: an affected or unaffected child does not determine what happens in the next pregnancy.

Doctors call this autosomal recessive inheritance. Below, we explain the words and the familiar four-box diagram. We also look at why your family’s actual reports matter, what a negative carrier screen can miss and which questions to take to a genetics appointment. None of this is a reason to blame either parent.
summary: The common SMN1-related form usually follows an autosomal recessive pattern.
The familiar one-in-four chance assumes both partners are carriers and applies separately to each pregnancy.
Family results need interpretation; a diagram cannot establish anyone’s genotype.

sections.title: Genes, chromosomes and the meaning of “recessive”
paragraphs: Genes provide instructions used by the body. SMN1 is involved in making survival motor neuron protein, which is important for motor neurons. These nerve cells carry signals to muscles. In common SMN1-related SMA, disease-causing changes involving both copies can lead to insufficient functional protein and the condition.

People generally inherit one copy of each chromosome from each parent. “Autosomal” means the usual inheritance pattern is not linked to the sex chromosomes. “Recessive” means that one working copy is usually sufficient to prevent this form of SMA, which is why carriers can be healthy and unaware of their status.

The explanation is specific to this genetic form. Other rare conditions can include muscle weakness or use similar terminology. Ask the clinician to name the diagnosis and gene in full rather than applying the same inheritance chart to every disorder described as muscle wasting or spinal atrophy.

sections.title: What being a carrier means
paragraphs: A typical carrier has one working SMN1 copy and one affected copy. They can pass either copy to a child without having SMA themselves. Carrying a genetic change is not a choice or a sign that the person did something wrong during pregnancy. Both men and women can be carriers.

Because carriers are generally healthy, there may be no known family history. A condition can appear in a family when two people happen to pass relevant changes to the same child. A healthy appearance, sporting ability or absence of a previous diagnosis does not establish a person’s carrier status.

Carrier testing asks about that status; diagnostic testing asks whether findings explain a person’s suspected condition. The purposes should be kept separate. A parent’s screen does not replace assessment of a child with symptoms, and a child’s diagnosis should lead to appropriate professional advice about family implications.

sections.title: When both partners are carriers: the four possibilities
paragraphs: In the usual carrier-by-carrier situation, a child may inherit the working copy from both parents, a working copy from one and an affected copy from the other, or an affected copy from both. These possibilities explain the familiar one-in-four, two-in-four and one-in-four pattern.

For each pregnancy, the chance is 25% of an affected child, 50% of a child who is a carrier without having SMA, and 25% of a child who has not inherited either parent’s relevant affected copy. These figures describe the standard scenario before the individual pregnancy’s genetic status is known.

Read the diagram as possible combinations, rather than a test result for an existing child or pregnancy. Your reports need to establish whether the standard carrier-by-carrier situation applies. If a clinician gives a different explanation, ask what finding changes it. A diagram is a useful teaching aid, but cannot replace information about the particular family being assessed.

rows: Unaffected, not a carrier of these parental changes

sections.title: Why the chance does not reset after one child
paragraphs: Genetic inheritance does not allocate one outcome to each birth in a set of four. A family with an affected child is not guaranteed that its next three children will be unaffected. A family with several unaffected children has not demonstrated that the underlying carrier situation has disappeared.

The same principle applies in the other direction: a one-in-four chance does not establish that a particular pregnancy is affected. A probability before testing and a diagnostic finding are different kinds of information. The appropriate tests can address a specific pregnancy or person within their scope.

It can still feel as though a previous outcome ought to change the next one, even after the percentage has been explained. Ask the genetics professional to go through it again using your reports. You can also ask how testing options relate to your future plans. Needing another explanation does not mean you have failed to understand something simple.

sections.title: What if only one partner is a known carrier?
paragraphs: Knowing one person is a carrier does not establish the other person’s status. The genetics team can discuss appropriate partner testing, using relevant family information. A test for another inherited condition or a routine health check is not an SMA carrier result.

If the other partner has a negative screen, the remaining risk depends on the method and clinical context. “Negative” usually means the targeted finding was not detected within the assay’s scope, not that every possible carrier state has been excluded. Ask for the laboratory’s interpretation and the meaning of residual risk.

Avoid using a population carrier frequency as if it were a confirmed diagnosis for a partner. It may be part of a professional risk estimate, but it does not tell you the person’s actual genotype. The purpose of further advice is to clarify what can be known and what remains uncertain.

sections.title: Two SMN1 copies do not always mean the same arrangement
paragraphs: Some people have two SMN1 copies on one chromosome and none on the other. This 2+0 configuration can be missed by a screen that counts total copies without distinguishing their arrangement. The total may look like the usual 1+1 pattern, despite a different implication for carrier status.

Ask what the analysis could detect and what remained outside its scope. Some laboratories use additional markers or other information to refine the result. The number two alone cannot establish a 2+0 arrangement. A family history may also change which question needs answering next. Keep the limitations with the report; they help explain the meaning of the result, rather than being disposable small print.

Ancestry-related estimates also need care. African ancestry is diverse, and a risk calculated from one studied population is not automatically the exact risk for a Nigerian individual. Ask the laboratory and genetics professional which assumptions support the explanation of your report.

source.title: Milligan and colleagues: interpreting silent-carrier results

sections.title: SMN1 and SMN2 have different roles
paragraphs: SMN2 is a related gene that can contribute some functional protein. Its copy number can influence the condition’s expression and is relevant to specialist discussions. It is not interchangeable with SMN1 and should not be counted as though all copies of the two genes perform the same role.

A family may hear an SMN1 result in a carrier discussion and an SMN2 result in a diagnosis or treatment discussion. Keep the full reports so the professional can explain which question each finding addresses. A remembered statement that someone has “two copies” is incomplete without knowing which gene, analysis and interpretation were involved.

SMN2 copy number is not a reliable personal countdown or a complete prediction of milestones. Ask what it adds to the individual assessment and what it cannot establish. The person’s current health and care needs still require examination and follow-up.

sections.title: What a child’s diagnosis means for parents and relatives
paragraphs: A confirmed SMN1-related diagnosis in a child often leads to parental testing and a genetics discussion. The usual recessive pattern is a valuable explanation, but the exact findings need confirmation. Less common situations, including a new genetic change, can affect interpretation. Avoid declaring every parent’s or relative’s status from a general rule alone.

Bring the child’s complete report and any earlier parental screens. The professional can decide which further analysis would clarify the family situation. This is especially important when later events appear inconsistent with an older negative screen or an informal explanation the family relied on.

Ask which relatives could benefit from advice and how the relevant information should be shared. Consent and privacy matter. A family letter may explain the important finding without distributing personal identifiers or unrelated medical details. Relatives should have their own opportunity to ask questions and decide about appropriate testing.

sections.title: Planning a pregnancy or discussing a current one
paragraphs: Before pregnancy, counselling can provide time to interpret results, consider partner testing and understand available reproductive options. A family may seek information without committing to any procedure. The options and practical pathway depend on the actual findings, local services and the family’s values.

During pregnancy, tell the maternity or genetics team the stage of pregnancy and the result that raised the question. Ask which discussions are time-sensitive and distinguish screening from diagnostic testing. A routine reassuring pregnancy screen does not automatically settle every question about SMA.

If testing is proposed, ask what a positive, negative or uncertain result would mean and who explains it. The aim is informed choice, not pressure to follow another family’s decision. Use qualified local professionals for the available pathways rather than assuming information from another country applies unchanged.

source.title: ACOG: carrier screening for genetic conditions

sections.title: Explain inheritance without blame or stigma
paragraphs: Genetic terms can land differently in a distressed family. Calling a gene “faulty” may be heard as calling a person at fault. Explain what a carrier result means and say plainly that nobody chose what they inherited. The purpose of the conversation is to understand the findings, options and support available, rather than identify someone to accuse.

Avoid asking which side of a family is “to blame”. In the standard recessive pattern, the relevant inheritance involves both parents, and in every situation the purpose of testing is understanding rather than accusation. A genetics professional can help communicate a complex finding calmly and accurately.

Public awareness also needs consent. A child’s story does not make every relative’s reproductive information public property. Share general explanations freely, but obtain agreement before identifying someone’s carrier status or posting reports. The people described should retain control over private aspects of their lives.

sections.title: Questions for your next appointment
paragraphs: Prepare three questions: what do our confirmed results establish, what uncertainty remains and which next step would change the decision we need to make? Bring full reports and relevant family information. Label unknown details honestly rather than filling gaps from memory or assumptions.

Ask for a plain-language summary and repeat the explanation back. For example, “The one-in-four chance applies if this is our confirmed carrier situation, and each pregnancy is separate.” If the professional corrects that statement for your family, ask for the reason to be written down with the reports.

When Every Breath Matters tells how questions about genetics affected our family’s life. The story may make those questions feel less remote, particularly for a relative trying to understand. Take any question it raises about your own results to the genetics team. Their explanation should help you understand the report and what, if anything, you need to do next.

If you use the table below with a relative, begin by stating its assumptions: both parents are confirmed carriers in the standard recessive scenario. Then explain that each cell represents a possible combination, not a birth order. Ending with those two points helps prevent the diagram from becoming a misleading promise about the next pregnancy.

faqs.question: Is SMA inherited only from the mother?
faqs.answer: Not in the usual autosomal recessive pattern of SMN1-related SMA. Relevant changes are generally inherited through both parents, who may be healthy carriers. The family’s exact reports should be interpreted professionally, including less common situations. The explanation should never become a basis for blaming either parent.

faqs.question: Does one affected child guarantee the next child will be unaffected?
faqs.answer: No. In the standard carrier-by-carrier scenario, each pregnancy has the same one-in-four chance independently. Outcomes are not distributed in a fixed sequence of four births. A genetics professional can relate that general principle to the family’s confirmed findings and available testing options.

faqs.question: Can a family have SMA without knowing any previous affected relatives?
faqs.answer: Yes. Carriers can be healthy and unidentified, so a family may have no recognised earlier diagnosis. Absence of family history does not settle a concern about symptoms or establish carrier status. Ask which clinical assessment or test addresses the question you actually need answered.

faqs.question: Do two SMN1 copies exclude every carrier configuration?
faqs.answer: No. A total copy count may not distinguish one copy on each chromosome from a 2+0 arrangement, and methods have other limits. Ask about the exact assay and residual risk. The total alone neither proves silent-carrier status nor removes every possibility.

faqs.question: Does SMN2 copy number determine the inheritance chance?
faqs.answer: SMN1-related findings and the parents’ carrier situation are central to the usual inheritance discussion. SMN2 has a different role and can contribute information about the condition’s expression. Ask the professional to explain each gene separately rather than combining all copy numbers into one calculation.

faqs.question: Should we send relatives our full reports?
faqs.answer: Ask the genetics service what relatives need to know. It may be possible to share a short family letter instead of your full report. Ask permission before sharing someone else’s result, and leave relatives room to seek their own advice. Private identifiers and reproductive information do not belong in a public group.

checklist: Keep the complete laboratory report, including its method and limitations.
Record your family history and any previous test results.
Ask which person or service will explain the result and arrange follow-up.
Discuss partner or family testing with the genetics professional rather than interpreting results in isolation.
bookContext: The genetics became personal for our family. We tell that story in When Every Breath Matters, alongside the care, relationships and faith that shaped our experience. It may be a useful read for someone who wants to understand why these questions matter beyond a diagram.

title: SMA newborn screening in England: what parents need to know
excerpt: Understand England’s phased SMA newborn screening evaluation, blood spot testing, results, confirmatory assessment and questions for your maternity team.
intro: Is your baby’s blood spot sample being screened for SMA? In England, the answer depends on the laboratory during the phased NHS in-service evaluation that began in October 2026. Do not assume SMA was included simply because the heel-prick sample was taken. Ask your midwife or screening team to check.

The programme information linked below was checked in November 2026. Ask the local team about current arrangements as rollout continues. If you receive a concerning result, follow the specialist referral promptly. If your baby has symptoms, seek medical assessment whether or not SMA screening was offered.
summary: England’s SMA screening programme is being introduced in phases.
Confirm whether the laboratory processing the baby’s sample includes SMA.
A concerning screen needs prompt confirmation, and symptoms need assessment regardless of screening.

sections.title: What SMA newborn screening is trying to achieve
paragraphs: Screening aims to identify babies who may have the common SMN1-related form of spinal muscular atrophy before symptoms become established. That can allow earlier specialist assessment and a treatment discussion. It is a population screening pathway, not a replacement for examining an individual baby who is unwell or developing differently.

A screen asks whether the sample has a finding that needs follow-up. Diagnostic confirmation and assessment establish the next clinical steps. Parents should not have to work out the diagnosis from a laboratory phrase alone. A concerning result should connect the family to a service with responsibility for explaining it.

Ask three questions: was SMA included, what did the screen find and who will explain what happens next? A message saying the heel-prick test was done may answer only that a sample was taken. You can ask the screening service to check the actual conditions tested and explain any follow-up. You should not have to infer the answer from a general results message.

source.title: NHS England: SMA suspected after newborn screening

sections.title: Which laboratories are offering SMA screening?
paragraphs: The official timetable checked in November 2026 lists Birmingham from October 2026 and Manchester from December 2026, followed by additional laboratories in stages. It describes an England-wide offer expected by spring 2028. These are programme details, not confirmation that an individual baby’s sample has already been tested for SMA.

Use the linked official timetable for the full sequence and ask the maternity or screening service about your sample’s laboratory. Do not infer coverage simply from the town where you live or the hospital where the baby was born. A published future date and an operational local service are different things.

Check the date before sharing a screening announcement. A national plan can be in place while laboratories are joining at different times. If another parent asks whether their baby is covered, point them to the current timetable and their screening team. Avoid turning the start of rollout into a claim that every baby has already been screened.

source.title: NHS England: introduction of SMA newborn screening

sections.title: England’s programme is not a single UK-wide arrangement
paragraphs: Health services and screening arrangements are not identical across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. An article about England should not be used as proof of the pathway elsewhere. Parents in another UK nation should ask their maternity or screening service and use the relevant official local information.

If your family moves around the time of birth or sampling, ask who holds responsibility for the sample and result. Make sure the service has current contact details. Do not assume the receiving area automatically knows which screening was offered or where the specimen was processed.

You can ask: “Which laboratory processed our sample, did it include SMA and who can explain the result?” Write down the answer if you have been unsure about what was included. The screening team can check the sample’s actual details, which a general announcement about national rollout will not tell you.

sections.title: How it connects with the blood spot test
paragraphs: The SMA screen uses the newborn blood spot sample where the programme is operating. The official parent information describes the sample being taken around day five. Your maternity team should explain the actual appointment and consent process for your baby, including any individual circumstances affecting sampling.

Ask which conditions are included and how you will receive the results. If the sample needs repeating, ask why, who arranges it and what happens next. A repeat request is not a diagnosis; the screening service should explain its meaning rather than leave the family to infer it.

Check that the service has your current phone number and address. Tell it if you need an interpreter, another format or help with access. If you are unsure whether a call or message is genuine, use the service’s official contact to check promptly. That lets you verify it without putting off follow-up that may be important.

source.title: NHS England: SMA suspected after newborn screening

sections.title: What an “SMA suspected” result means
paragraphs: The official parent leaflet explains that a result described as “SMA suspected” needs further tests and urgent specialist assessment. It is important information, but the screening phrase should not be treated as a complete diagnosis or a prediction of every future care need.

If contacted, clarify the appointment details, named service, records required and contact for questions. The specialist may be based beyond your local hospital. Ask about practical arrangements promptly, especially if travel or childcare for other children could affect attendance. Tell the service about a barrier rather than simply missing the appointment.

A baby may look well when the call comes. That does not make follow-up unnecessary or show that the screen is wrong. Screening is intended to find concerns that may not yet be obvious in ordinary daily life. The clinical team should explain what is being checked and how quickly the pathway needs to move.

source.title: NHS England: SMA suspected after newborn screening

sections.title: What happens at the specialist appointment?
paragraphs: Ask the team which analysis will confirm or clarify the screening finding and who explains the result. A clinical assessment also looks at the baby’s present health. The report and examination answer related questions, and the plan should make clear what has been established at each stage.

Bring available screening information and any relevant family genetic reports. If a parent previously had a negative carrier screen, provide the actual document rather than using it to dismiss the newborn concern. Screening methods and their purposes differ, and a professional should explain the relationship between the findings.

Before leaving, ask who does what next. Will the team call with a result, or should you book another visit? When should you expect to hear, and whom should you call if you do not? Write those details down. You may still be taking in the medical explanation, but you should not be left uncertain about the next appointment.

sections.title: Early treatment evidence supports prompt assessment
paragraphs: Studies such as NURTURE have followed babies who began treatment before symptoms. They contribute to evidence that early identification can change outcomes. This is a reason to take the referral seriously, not a promise that every baby will have the same development or need the same treatment.

Different studies and medicines involve different populations, eligibility criteria and follow-up. Ask the specialist which evidence relates to the baby’s confirmed findings and current situation. Avoid ranking treatments from unrelated trial percentages or another family’s social-media account.

A treatment discussion should also identify supportive care and monitoring needs. A baby may require assessment of breathing, feeding or other areas alongside consideration of a medicine. Ask which actions are needed now and how the team will coordinate them, rather than assume that one treatment decision answers every care question.

sections.title: If SMA screening was not offered in your area
paragraphs: Ask the maternity or screening team to confirm the position before assuming a test was omitted accidentally. A phased programme can mean that different laboratories are at different stages. The official guidance should explain the current route, and your local service should identify what was offered to your baby.

If you have a family history, an existing carrier concern or symptoms in the baby, tell the appropriate clinician. Those are individual clinical questions and should not be left to wait for a population rollout. Ask which assessment or genetic advice is needed in your circumstances.

If considering private testing, first establish the question, test scope, laboratory, result timing and follow-up arrangement with a qualified professional. Paying for a product that mentions SMA does not automatically reproduce the NHS screening and specialist-referral pathway. The full route matters as much as the analysis itself.

sections.title: A reassuring screen does not replace attention to symptoms
paragraphs: If your baby develops unusual weakness, feeding difficulty, a change in movement or another concern, seek assessment. Tell the clinician what screening was done and bring the result if available. The professional can decide whether diagnostic investigation is appropriate despite earlier screening information.

Do not assume every concerning symptom is SMA, either. Several conditions can affect a baby’s movement or feeding, and a clinical examination is needed. The role of a parent is to describe the change and obtain help, not to prove a particular diagnosis using an online list.

Severe breathing difficulty, choking, blue or grey colouring, or sudden marked difficulty waking needs emergency medical care. Do not wait for screening paperwork, a genetic result or a support-chat reply. Routine information and urgent assessment serve different purposes, and one should not delay the other.

sections.title: Consent, records and questions for the service
paragraphs: Ask for an explanation of the offer and the choice being made. You should understand which test is involved, how results are communicated and where to obtain more information. If you need an interpreter or another accessible format, tell the service rather than relying on a relative’s partial translation of a complex explanation.

Keep the sample date, result information and relevant service contact together. Record a question if something remains unclear: “Did this include SMA?” is a legitimate enquiry even after a routine results message. If different professionals give conflicting answers, ask the screening service to clarify the actual sample pathway.

Share medical documents only through the channel the service requests and with the people who need them. Relatives helping with travel or meals do not need copies of a baby’s complete genetic records. Practical support and privacy can coexist.

If a call introduces too many unfamiliar terms at once, ask the person to begin with what you need to do now. Is there an appointment to attend or a document to send? Then ask when and where you can hear the fuller explanation. It is reasonable to need more time, while still knowing the immediate step and how to contact the team.

sections.title: Supporting parents during an unexpected referral
paragraphs: An unexpected screening call can change the atmosphere of the first weeks with a baby. Supporters can help by listening, offering one practical task and avoiding either alarming predictions or sweeping reassurance. Ask what the family wants shared before forwarding news or contacting a wider community.

Parents may need to hear an explanation more than once. Taking notes, bringing a chosen supporter and asking the team to confirm a plain-language summary can help. The need for another explanation does not mean the family is failing to understand or cooperate.

An unexpected referral can leave relatives unsure what to say. Our family’s story in When Every Breath Matters may help them understand some of the care and worry around SMA. It cannot tell them what will happen to another baby. The most helpful response is to listen to the parents, respect their privacy and offer something they would welcome.

faqs.question: Is every baby in England already screened for SMA?
faqs.answer: Do not assume that. The official information checked on 17 November 2026 describes a phased evaluation beginning in October 2026. Ask the screening or maternity service whether the laboratory processing your baby’s sample includes SMA, and use the current official timetable rather than an older headline.

faqs.question: Is the blood spot test itself a confirmed SMA diagnosis?
faqs.answer: A concerning screen needs further testing and specialist assessment. The official parent information distinguishes screening from confirmation. Follow the contact instructions promptly and ask what the next analysis will establish. A screening phrase alone does not predict every aspect of a baby’s future health.

faqs.question: My baby looks well. Should we still attend after a concerning result?
faqs.answer: Yes, follow the specialist referral instructions. Screening can identify a concern before symptoms are obvious. Looking well does not establish that the result is wrong or make the appointment unnecessary. Ask the responsible team about timing and tell it promptly about any practical barrier to attending.

faqs.question: What if our sample was processed in another region?
faqs.answer: Ask the screening service which laboratory processed the sample and who holds the result. During rollout, that detail matters more than assuming coverage from your home postcode. Check that your contact details are current, particularly if you have moved. The service can explain which screening was offered and any follow-up required.

faqs.question: Can we ignore symptoms after a reassuring screening result?
faqs.answer: No. A new clinical concern deserves assessment on its own merits. Tell the clinician what screening was performed and provide the result. Severe breathing difficulty, choking or sudden serious illness needs urgent care rather than waiting for a routine screening discussion.

faqs.question: Does this article describe all four UK nations?
faqs.answer: No. It focuses on England’s phased programme. Parents elsewhere in the UK should use their relevant maternity and screening services for current local arrangements. Do not assume that an England-specific timetable, referral route or announcement applies unchanged across the UK.

checklist: Write down the concern or decision you most need help with.
Bring the complete genetic report and relevant care records.
Ask what needs to happen next, who arranges it and how to follow up.
Discuss practical barriers such as travel, work, school or equipment before leaving the appointment.
bookContext: When Every Breath Matters follows our family’s experience of SMA across Nigeria, Dubai and the UK. For relatives who want to understand more of life around a diagnosis, the book offers a personal story to read alongside listening to the family they are supporting.
